documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
47F transferring in. Her old PCP is retiring and she wanted somewhere she could reach by text. Records requested.

PMH
- Hep C, genotype 1a, found 2011 on routine labs. Started an interferon-based regimen around 2012 and stopped partway through. Never re-treated.
- HTN, on HCTZ 25 for a few years. Checks at the pharmacy machine occasionally, usually 130s.
- Alcohol use disorder: drank daily, heavily, for more than ten years. Quit early 2018, no relapse. Not in a program now; says she doesn't need one.
PSH: lap chole 2014 (age 42).
Meds: HCTZ 25 mg daily.
Allergies: none known.
FH: mother HTN, breast cancer at 65. Father had cirrhosis from drinking. Maternal aunt had lung cancer and never smoked. Brother has type 2 DM.
SH: office administrator. Single. Never smoked, no secondhand exposure. No alcohol since 2018. No drugs.

ROS: no fatigue, no jaundice, no abdominal swelling, no headaches, no chest pain. Otherwise negative.

Exam: BP and vitals per flowsheet. Comfortable. Anicteric. No spider angiomata. Oropharynx clear. Neck supple, no adenopathy. Heart regular rate, no murmur. Lungs clear bilaterally. Abdomen soft, nontender, well-healed laparoscopic scars, liver edge not palpable, no splenomegaly, no fluid wave. No edema. Skin without rash.

A/P
1. Chronic hep C: CMP, CBC, HCV RNA quant today. Hep B sAg and sAb. Starting Twinrix series today since no record of hepatitis A or B vaccination; she'll come back in a month and at 6 months.
2. HTN: a little high in the office today, pharmacy readings 130s. Continue HCTZ 25, recheck next visit.
3. AUD in remission: AUDIT-C 0. Congratulated her on 18 months.
4. Health maintenance: Tdap today. HIV screen with labs. Lipids, A1c (brother with DM), TSH. Last mammogram 2018 per patient, Pap 2017; will confirm on records. Colon screening to discuss at the physical next year.
Follow up 6 months, sooner with lab issues.

documents.title: Your lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Hi Julie,

Your labs are back. Kidney function, sugar, thyroid and blood counts are normal. A1c is 5.6, top end of normal, worth watching with your brother's diabetes. Cholesterol is acceptable and doesn't need a medicine.

Liver enzymes (AST and ALT) are mildly up, which is what we'd expect with active hepatitis C. Bilirubin and albumin are normal. The hepatitis C virus level is detectable, so the infection is still active. HIV screen negative. Hepatitis B: you've never had it, and you're not immune either, which is why the Twinrix series matters. See you in about a month for dose two.

PCP

Her home cuff read very high during one episode, and between episodes it has been running above her usual. No chest pain, no syncope, no weight change, no tremor, no new medicines or supplements, no decongestants, no caffeine change. No alcohol.

Exam: BP high as charted, recheck similar. Appears well between episodes. No thyromegaly. Heart regular. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, no bruit, no mass. Skin warm.

A/P
Paroxysmal headache, palpitations, diaphoresis with newly uncontrolled HTN. Pheochromocytoma has to be excluded first; also thyroid. Plasma free metanephrines and normetanephrines (drawn seated, she's not on anything that interferes), TSH, BMP.

documents.title: Results call
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Called pt. Plasma free metanephrine 480 and normetanephrine 1,350 pg/mL, both well above the lab's upper limits; TSH normal. Glucose 110, K 3.5, creatinine 0.9. reports.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
reports.text:
Technique: helical CT of the abdomen and pelvis after IV contrast, portal venous phase, with delayed adrenal images.
Adrenals: 3.0 cm heterogeneous, avidly enhancing left adrenal mass without macroscopic fat; attenuation and enhancement are not those of a lipid-rich adenoma. Right adrenal normal.
Liver normal in size and contour without focal lesion. Gallbladder surgically absent; no biliary dilation. Spleen, pancreas and kidneys normal. No lymphadenopathy. No ascites. Bowel, bladder, uterus and ovaries unremarkable. Bones unremarkable.
reports.conclusion: 3 cm left adrenal mass with features suggesting pheochromocytoma in the setting of elevated metanephrines. No other abnormality.

documents.title: Endocrinology Consultation
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
Outside endocrinology group
Date of visit: 01/02/2023
Re: Julie Lambert, DOB 01/27/1972

Dear Doctor,
Thank you for asking us to see Ms. Lambert, 50, for spells and a left adrenal mass.

For roughly half a year she has had attacks of headache, palpitations and sweating, sometimes with a feeling of impending doom, often brought on by exertion or stress. Background: chronic hepatitis C genotype 1a since 2011 with an unfinished antiviral course, hypertension on hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, alcohol use disorder in remission since 2018, cholecystectomy 2014. NKDA. Never smoker. Mother with hypertension and breast cancer; father with alcohol-related cirrhosis; maternal aunt with lung cancer; brother with type 2 diabetes. She works as an office administrator.

Exam: BP 170/95 in clinic. Well nourished, mildly distressed. Skin notably moist. No abdominal bruit or palpable mass.

Data: your labs (glucose 110 mg/dL, potassium 3.5, creatinine 0.9; plasma free metanephrines elevated) and CT (3 cm left adrenal mass, features of pheochromocytoma). We added a 24-hour urine collection, completed 01/05: urinary metanephrines and normetanephrines both elevated.

Impression: pheochromocytoma, left adrenal, biochemically and radiographically confirmed.

Plan:
1. Surgical resection: referred to endocrine surgery for laparoscopic left adrenalectomy.
2. Alpha blockade: doxazosin 2 mg daily started, liberal salt and fluids, home BP twice daily. We will adjust before surgery.
3. Continue HCTZ for now.
4. Postoperative plasma metanephrines 6-8 weeks after surgery, then yearly.

Sincerely,
Endocrinology

conditions.label: Benign neoplasm of left adrenal gland

reports.text:
Specimen: left adrenal gland, laparoscopic adrenalectomy.
Gross: adrenal gland 28 g containing a well-circumscribed tan-red mass, 3.0 x 2.7 x 2.5 cm.
Microscopic: nested (zellballen) chromaffin cell neoplasm, chromogranin and synaptophysin positive, with S100-positive sustentacular cells. Tumor confined to the adrenal gland. Margins negative. No lymphovascular invasion identified.
reports.conclusion: Pheochromocytoma, 3.0 cm, confined to the adrenal gland; margins negative.

documents.title: Nephrology Consultation
documents.author: nephrology
documents.body:
Outside nephrology group
Date of service: 01/01/2024 (holiday urgent session)

Dear Doctor,
Thanks for the same-week referral of Ms. Lambert, a 51-year-old with longstanding hepatitis C, a resected pheochromocytoma and lichen planus.

She describes two weeks of aching, symmetric pain in the wrists and knees, a rash over the lower legs, fatigue beyond her usual, and episodic tingling of the hands and feet. No recent infection and no new medication.

Medications: hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily; acetaminophen as needed. NKDA.

Exam: T 37.2 C, BP 130/80, pulse 78. Palpable purpura over both legs. Joints without synovitis.

Data: your 12/22 labs: creatinine 1.2 (baseline 0.9), urinalysis with protein and blood, normal CBC, mildly elevated AST/ALT. Today: C4 low with normal C3; rheumatoid factor positive; serum protein electrophoresis shows a polyclonal gammopathy, no monoclonal band. Serum cryoglobulins sent, kept warm, result to follow.

Impression: picture of mixed cryoglobulinemia secondary to hepatitis C with skin, joint, nerve and kidney involvement.

Plan: await cryoglobulins. Recheck creatinine and urinalysis in about 6 weeks; this can be done with you. Acetaminophen rather than NSAIDs. We will send an addendum.

Date of visit: 06/10/2024

Dear Doctor,
Thank you for referring Ms. Lambert, 52, for treatment of chronic hepatitis C, now complicated by mixed cryoglobulinemia.

Hepatitis C genotype 1a was found in 2011. An interferon-based course around 2012 was stopped partway through, and she has had no treatment since. Alcohol use disorder, abstinent since 2018. Nephrology diagnosed mixed type II cryoglobulinemia in January (purpura, joint pain, tingling, creatinine 1.2 with protein and blood in the urine); the purpura has faded and creatinine was 1.1 in February. Lichen planus. Pheochromocytoma resected 2023. Cholecystectomy 2014.

Medications: hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily; acetaminophen as needed. NKDA.

Exam: anicteric. No spider angiomata or palmar erythema. Abdomen soft, liver edge not palpable, no splenomegaly, no fluid wave. No edema. No asterixis.

Labs today: HCV RNA 1,860,000 IU/mL, genotype 1a. AST 55, ALT 67, platelets 248,000. FIB-4 1.41, no advanced fibrosis. Hepatitis B surface antigen and core antibody negative.

Impression: chronic hepatitis C genotype 1a with prior interferon exposure, no advanced fibrosis, with HCV-related mixed cryoglobulinemia. Antiviral treatment addresses both.

Plan:
1. Sofosbuvir 400 mg/velpatasvir 100 mg, one tablet daily for 12 weeks. No interactions with her current medicines; no antacids or acid-reducing medicines, and check with us before any new prescription or supplement. Our specialty pharmacy will ship once insurance approves; we will write when she starts.
2. No routine labs during treatment.
3. HCV RNA 12 weeks or more after the last dose; this can be drawn at your office. Please send us the result.
4. No alcohol.

Sincerely,
Hepatology

documents.title: Emergency Department Record with GI Consultation
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital emergency department
Visit: 12/20/2024, 14:05-21:40

Chief complaint: tired, not eating, dark urine.

HPI: 52-year-old woman with hepatitis C genotype 1a (12 weeks of sofosbuvir/velpatasvir, last dose 09/29/2024), HCV-related cryoglobulinemia and alcohol use disorder in sustained remission, started isoniazid for latent TB six weeks ago. For two weeks: fatigue, anorexia, tea-colored urine. No alcohol. No travel. No known hepatitis contacts. No acetaminophen beyond the occasional tablet.

Medications: isoniazid 300 mg daily, pyridoxine 50 mg daily, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily. NKDA.

Exam: afebrile, hemodynamically stable. Scleral icterus. Mild right upper quadrant tenderness without guarding. No hepatomegaly or splenomegaly. No peripheral edema. Alert, no asterixis.

Labs: AST 450 U/L, ALT 520 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 120 U/L, total bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 2.1 mg/dL, INR 1.1. Hepatitis A IgM, hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis B core IgM negative. HCV RNA not detected.

RUQ ultrasound: liver normal in size without focal lesion; no intra- or extrahepatic biliary dilation; gallbladder surgically absent; spleen normal in size; no ascites.

GI consult (ED): hepatocellular injury pattern with jaundice, timing typical for isoniazid hepatotoxicity; HCV RNA negative after her recent hepatitis C treatment, so not a viral relapse. INR normal, no encephalopathy; safe for outpatient management.

Disposition: isoniazid and pyridoxine discontinued, do not rechallenge. Discharged home. Repeat liver tests with primary care within 10 days; return for confusion, bleeding, vomiting or worsening jaundice.

Diagnosis: isoniazid-induced liver injury (drug-induced liver injury).

Regional hospital, gastroenterology service (MICU 07/02-07/04, then ward)
Admitted 07/02/2025, discharged 07/07/2025

Patient: Julie Lambert, 53

Presentation: several episodes of vomiting bright red blood over 4 hours. For about 6 months, progressive abdominal swelling and fatigue; for the past few months, easy bruising and ankle swelling. Background: hepatitis C since 2011 (incomplete course in 2012; cured with sofosbuvir/velpatasvir in 2024) with mixed cryoglobulinemia, isoniazid liver injury in December 2024, resected pheochromocytoma, lichen planus, oral leukoplakia, hypertension. No alcohol since 2018 after more than a decade of daily drinking.

Admission exam: T 37.1 C, BP 94/60, HR 112, RR 20. Pale and fatigued. Scleral icterus. Spider angiomata across the chest. Abdomen distended with a fluid wave; spleen palpable; prominent tortuous veins radiating from the umbilicus. Rectal exam: no blood.

Admission labs: hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL, platelets 84,000/mm3, AST 162, ALT 94, alkaline phosphatase 188, total bilirubin 4.3, direct bilirubin 2.1, albumin 2.5, INR 1.7. Renal function normal.

Hospital course:
1. Acute esophageal variceal hemorrhage. Octreotide infusion, IV pantoprazole, ceftriaxone. Urgent upper endoscopy on 07/02: markedly dilated varices in the distal esophagus with stigmata of recent bleeding; 5 bands placed. Stomach and duodenum normal. Octreotide for 72 hours. No further bleeding. Not transfused. Ceftriaxone changed to oral ciprofloxacin to complete 7 days. Discharge hemoglobin 8.9.
2. Cirrhosis due to hepatitis C (virus cured 2024) with portal hypertension and ascites, newly recognized. Ultrasound with Doppler: nodular liver, splenomegaly 15.2 cm, moderate ascites, patent portal vein, no liver mass. Diagnostic paracentesis: ascitic neutrophils 110/mm3, ascitic albumin 0.9 g/dL (SAAG 1.6), culture no growth; no SBP. Diuretics started. No encephalopathy.
3. Hypertension: hydrochlorothiazide stopped given admission hypotension and new diuretics.

Discharge medications:
- Propranolol 20 mg twice daily (new)
- Spironolactone 100 mg daily (new)
- Furosemide 40 mg daily (new)
- Pantoprazole 40 mg daily for 14 days (new)
- Ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 2 more days (new)
- STOP hydrochlorothiazide
Allergies: NKDA.

Instructions: 2 g sodium diet; no alcohol; no NSAIDs; acetaminophen no more than 2 g a day. Weigh daily.
Follow-up: primary care within 1 week with BMP, CBC, liver panel and INR; repeat upper endoscopy with banding in about 4 weeks (scheduled 07/30).

Right lower lobe mass with 3 months of cough and 10 lb weight loss in a never smoker with cirrhosis: needs CT and tissue promptly. Regional hospital, pulmonary medicine service
Admitted 12/30/2025 (direct admission from primary care), discharged 01/02/2026

Reason for admission: 3-month persistent cough and unintentional 10-lb weight loss with a right lower lobe mass on chest radiograph.

Background: cirrhosis from hepatitis C (cured 2024) with esophageal varices (bled July 2025, banded to eradication), mixed cryoglobulinemia, isoniazid liver injury 2024, resected pheochromocytoma, lichen planus, oral leukoplakia, hypertension. Never smoker, no secondhand smoke exposure. Maternal aunt with lung cancer.

Medications on admission: propranolol 20 mg BID, spironolactone 100 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily. NKDA.

Exam: afebrile, BP 130/85, HR 78, RR 16. Decreased breath sounds over the right lower lobe; no wheezes, rales or rhonchi.

Course: CT chest showed a solitary 2.5 cm spiculated peripheral right lower lobe nodule without lymphadenopathy or effusion. CT-guided core biopsy 12/31 after platelet and INR check, without complication. Pathology: adenocarcinoma, TTF-1 positive.

Diagnosis: non-small cell lung cancer, adenocarcinoma, right lower lobe.

Plan: outpatient PET-CT and MRI brain for staging (scheduled 01/06 and 01/07); thoracic surgery consultation 01/08. Molecular testing sent on the biopsy. Discharge medications unchanged.

reports.text: MRI brain, staging for lung adenocarcinoma, performed with and without gadolinium. No enhancing lesion. No mass effect, hemorrhage or acute infarct. Ventricles and sulci normal for age.

documents.title: ED and Hospital Discharge Summary
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital
ED arrival 01/25/2026 10:52; admitted to medicine; discharged 01/28/2026

Presentation: 53-year-old woman with stage IIIB non-small cell lung cancer, 10 days after VATS right lower lobectomy (01/15), largely bedbound since surgery, with 2 hours of sudden shortness of breath and sharp chest pain worse with deep breaths, plus a mild cough bringing up scant blood-tinged sputum. Also: cirrhosis from hepatitis C with eradicated varices, mixed cryoglobulinemia, resected pheochromocytoma, hypertension.

ED exam: anxious. RR 28, HR 110, BP 130/85, SpO2 89% on room air. Decreased breath sounds at the right base without wheezes or crackles. Remainder unremarkable.

ED data: arterial blood gas on room air pH 7.48, PaCO2 30, PaO2 70, HCO3 24. D-dimer elevated. Troponin and BNP normal. ECG sinus tachycardia. Chest film: no acute process, expected post-lobectomy change. CT pulmonary angiogram: acute segmental emboli in the left lower lobe, no right heart strain.

Course: oxygen by nasal cannula briefly, weaned to room air by day 2. Anticoagulation with enoxaparin 1 mg/kg (60 mg) every 12 hours; low-molecular-weight heparin chosen over oral agents given cirrhosis and active cancer. Platelets 90s. No bleeding. Discharge SpO2 95% on room air.

Diagnosis: acute pulmonary embolism, postoperative.

Discharge medications: enoxaparin 60 mg subcutaneously every 12 hours (new); propranolol 20 mg BID; spironolactone 100 mg daily; furosemide 40 mg daily; acetaminophen as needed, max 2 g/day.
Allergies: NKDA.
Follow-up: primary care within 1 week with CBC; oncology as scheduled. Duration of anticoagulation per oncology, at least 6 months.

Breathing much better. Using acetaminophen once or twice a day for the incisions. No more blood in the sputum. Doing the enoxaparin shots herself into the belly twice a day, no bleeding. No black stools. Oncology appointment 2/11.

Meds: enoxaparin 60 mg q12h, propranolol 20 BID, spironolactone 100, furosemide 40, acetaminophen PRN (max 2 g/day). NKDA.

Exam: BP 118/74, sat as charted on room air. Port sites healing well. Breath sounds reduced at the right base, left clear. Heart regular. Abdomen soft, no fluid wave. Calves soft, nontender, no edema.

A/P
1. Pulmonary embolism: on enoxaparin; CBC today for platelets.
2. Stage IIIB lung adenocarcinoma s/p lobectomy: oncology 2/11.
3. Cirrhosis: labs today. She's due for liver cancer surveillance; ordered ultrasound and AFP for March once she's moving better.
4. Varices eradicated: surveillance EGD in May; continue propranolol.
Med rec complete. See her in 2-3 months, sooner as needed.

Regional cancer center, thoracic oncology
Date of visit: 02/11/2026

Ms. Lambert, 54, never smoker, underwent VATS right lower lobectomy on 01/15/2026 for adenocarcinoma: 2.5 cm with a separate same-lobe nodule and one positive subcarinal node, pT3 pN2 M0, stage IIIB. Margins negative. EGFR exon 19 deletion; ALK negative. Postoperative PE on 01/25, on enoxaparin.

Comorbidity: hepatitis C cirrhosis, Child-Pugh B7, eradicated varices, platelets in the 90s. Mixed cryoglobulinemia. NKDA.

Exam: ECOG 1. Healing port sites. Lungs with reduced breath sounds at the right base.

Discussion: adjuvant platinum-based chemotherapy is not being offered given her cirrhosis and low platelets. With an EGFR exon 19 deletion, adjuvant osimertinib is recommended; plan 3 years if tolerated. Baseline echocardiogram and ECG before starting.

Plan:
1. Echo and ECG this month; start osimertinib 80 mg daily once reviewed.
2. CBC and liver tests monthly for the first three months, then every 3 months; may be drawn with primary care.
3. Enoxaparin 60 mg every 12 hours; we will prescribe it from here on. Duration at least 6 months and while on cancer treatment.
4. CT chest every 6 months.
